semantic_correction.stem: An adult ICU RN is caring for one unstable client receiving continuous renal replacement therapy and frequent vasoactive-infusion titration. A second critically ill admission is assigned to the RN. Which response best applies current critical-care staffing principles?

options.A: Accept the second patient because a two-patient assignment fits the usual staffing plan, then report workload concerns if care becomes delayed.
options.B: Report the current workload to the charge nurse and request assignment reassessment before accepting responsibility for the second critically ill patient.
options.C: Tell the charge nurse the assignment should remain one-to-one because CRRT itself determines staffing, without considering the rest of the workload.
options.D: Ask another bedside nurse to complete selected high-acuity tasks informally so the second patient can be added without changing the formal assignment.

semantic_correction.rationale: AACN's 2024 Standards for Appropriate Staffing in Adult Critical Care state that, for every shift, patient assignments should be based on an accurate assessment of the current nursing workload generated by each patient's needs and should align nurse competency with patient characteristics. AACN also states that organizational staffing plans should anticipate that critically ill or injured patients generally require about one nurse for two patients. Those statements are complementary rather than interchangeable: the 1:2 expectation is a planning standard, not a substitute for reassessing the actual workload of a specific assignment. In this scenario, the RN already has a highly resource-intensive unstable client. B appropriately communicates the current patient-generated workload and requests reassessment before assuming another critically ill patient; it does not presume that the second assignment must be rejected. A treats the usual numerical ratio as sufficient even though current workload may make the assignment unsafe. C turns one therapy into an automatic staffing rule instead of assessing the total workload. D creates an informal workaround rather than resolving the formal assignment through the staffing process. Therefore B is the uniquely best answer.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Apply critical-care staffing principles by communicating current patient-generated workload and requesting reassessment when a planned assignment may not match acuity and care demands, rather than using a numerical ratio or single therapy as the only staffing rule.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: retired passive recall of a 1:2 critical-care ratio and the conspicuous correct-answer length cue. Rebuilt the item around a bedside RN's responsibility to surface current patient-generated workload and request formal assignment reassessment when a planned second critical-care assignment may not match actual care demands.

audit_findings_append.finding: The original answer bundled the AACN workload/competency standard with the general 1:2 planning expectation and was much longer than distractors. The replacement makes workload reassessment the tested action and explicitly avoids treating either the 1:2 expectation or CRRT alone as an inflexible assignment rule.

near_duplicate_check.note: V2-Q0077 tests the RN's own education/competence limitation before an unfamiliar high-risk therapy. V2-Q0273 tests RN follow-up after abnormal data reported by a UAP. V2-Q0420 tests initial selection of a routine UAP task. V2-Q0427 tests workload- and acuity-based reassessment of a formal critical-care patient assignment.

option_audit.A: Plausible because AACN generally anticipates roughly 1:2 adult critical-care staffing, but the standards also require assignment decisions to reflect current patient-generated workload rather than relying on the number alone.
option_audit.B: Correct. It communicates the current workload and asks for formal reassessment without presuming that the second patient must automatically be refused.
option_audit.C: Plausible because CRRT can generate substantial nursing workload, but AACN does not support making one therapy by itself the staffing rule without considering the total assignment demands.
option_audit.D: Plausible teamwork response, but an informal redistribution of high-acuity tasks does not resolve whether the formal assignment itself is appropriate.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. B alone applies the source-supported requirement to reassess current patient-generated workload through the formal staffing process. A substitutes a general ratio for workload assessment, C substitutes one therapy for total workload, and D uses an informal workaround instead of reassessing the assignment.

cueing_check.note: Exact character counts were recalculated from the stored strings. All four options are within eleven characters and are parallel staffing responses; the correct answer is not conspicuously longer.
